polynesian-navigation.summary: Navigation by star paths, swell patterns, cloud formations and bird behaviour, carried in memory rather than on charts, and accurate enough to find islands a few kilometres wide across thousands of kilometres of ocean.
polynesian-navigation.significance: Dismissed for two centuries as accidental drift, it was vindicated in 1976 when Hokule'a sailed Hawaii to Tahiti with no instruments at all.
polynesian-navigation.note: Dismissed for two centuries as accidental drift, the tradition was vindicated in 1976 when Hokule'a sailed Hawaii to Tahiti without instruments.

chavin.summary: A religious centre in the Peruvian highlands whose art style spread across the Andes, apparently by pilgrimage rather than conquest.

scythians.summary: Mounted nomads ranging from the Black Sea to the Altai, known to Herodotus as unconquerable and to archaeology through frozen tombs that preserved their gold work, tattoos and horses.

homer.summary: The name attached to the Iliad and the Odyssey, composed orally and written down generations later.
homer.note: Whether Homer was one poet, several, or a name attached to a tradition is unresolved and probably unresolvable.

upanishads.display: c. 800–500 BCE to c. 300 BCE – 100 CE
upanishads.summary: Philosophical dialogues concluding the Vedic corpus, introducing brahman, atman and rebirth, and forming the basis of Vedanta.
upanishads.note: The oldest prose Upanishads, Brihadaranyaka and Chandogya, are usually put at c. 800-500 BCE and are pre-Buddhist. The verse Upanishads follow in the last centuries BCE, and Olivelle places the two late prose ones, Prashna and Mandukya, no earlier than about the start of the common era - which is where the bracket closes. He also warns that any dating of these texts more precise than a few centuries is a house of cards.

warring-states.summary: Five centuries of fragmentation and near-constant war that produced, paradoxically, the richest period in Chinese thought — Confucianism, Daoism, Legalism and Mohism all take shape here.

homeric-epics-written.summary: Composed and performed orally for generations, then fixed in writing once the Greek alphabet made it possible — and standardised in Athens in the sixth century BCE.

ramayana.summary: The Sanskrit epic of Rama, Sita and Ravana, ascribed to Valmiki. With the Mahabharata it is one of the two great epics of the subcontinent and the source of retellings across South and Southeast Asia.
ramayana.significance: Its reach is the point. Versions belong to Thailand, Indonesia, Cambodia and Laos, which makes it one of the few narratives to have become foundational to cultures that never shared a state.
ramayana.note: Books 2 to 6 are the oldest, with 1 and 7 added later. Brockington reads the language and puts the first oral stage around the fifth century BCE; Goldman argues the archetype cannot be much earlier than the start of the seventh, which is where the bracket opens. The text reached something like its present form by about the third century CE. Traditional accounts place the events far earlier, in the Treta Yuga.

valmiki.summary: The poet to whom the Ramayana is ascribed, and with it the sloka metre that Sanskrit narrative verse used for the next two thousand years.
valmiki.note: Tradition calls him the adi-kavi, the first poet, and the bracket is the period of the Ramayana's composition rather than a recorded life. The text grew over centuries, so a single author is a simplification the tradition itself makes.

sappho.summary: A lyric poet of Lesbos who wrote about desire in the first person at a time when Greek poetry was mostly public and heroic, and whose metre still carries her name.
sappho.note: Both dates are inferred from ancient testimony rather than recorded. Of nine books collected at Alexandria, one complete poem survives, with the rest in fragments and quotations.

thales.summary: Sought explanations for natural events in nature rather than in the gods, and is credited with predicting a solar eclipse.
thales.note: No contemporary record survives; the dates come from later Greek sources.

laozi.summary: The figure behind Daoism, which counsels acting in accordance with the grain of things rather than against it.
laozi.note: Possibly not a single historical person; the Daodejing may be a composite text assembled over generations.

sushruta.display: c. 600–100 BCE to c. 500 BCE – 100 CE
sushruta.summary: Associated with an early surgical tradition describing cataract couching, reconstructive skin grafts, and hundreds of instruments.
sushruta.note: The 600 BCE date still quoted everywhere comes from Hoernle in 1907 and has outlived its evidence. Meulenbeld's survey of Indian medical literature puts the composition of the Sushruta Samhita in the last centuries BCE at the earliest, with the surviving recension - the one Dalhana commented on - taking shape between the third and fifth centuries CE. A historical Sushruta behind the text is a reasonable inference and nothing more, so the bracket is wide.

mahavira.summary: The twenty-fourth and last Tirthankara of Jainism, who taught radical non-violence, non-attachment and the many-sidedness of truth.
mahavira.note: Jain tradition gives 599–527 BCE. Much modern scholarship places him later, roughly 497–425 BCE, partly by tying his dates to the revised chronology of the Buddha.

texts.title: Jainism texts at the Internet Sacred Text Archive

pythagoras.summary: Founded a school that treated number and ratio as the underlying structure of reality, including the relationship between string length and musical pitch.
pythagoras.note: The man and his school are hard to separate; most attributed results may belong to followers.

buddha.summary: Founder of Buddhism, who taught a middle path between asceticism and indulgence in the Gangetic plain of the Mahajanapada era.
buddha.significance: The dates matter more than they look. Shifting him a century changes what he was responding to, and it moves the Pali Canon's four-century gap along with him.
buddha.note: The traditional "long chronology" gives 563–483 BCE; most modern scholarship prefers a "short chronology" placing his death nearer 400 BCE.

confucius.summary: Taught that social order grows from personal character, ritual propriety and obligations running in both directions between ruler and ruled.
confucius.significance: A philosophy of obligation rather than belief, which shaped Chinese governance through the examination system for two thousand years.

achaemenid-empire.summary: The first Persian empire, stretching from the Indus to the Aegean and administered through satrapies and the Royal Road.

heraclitus.summary: Held that everything is in flux and that opposites depend on each other, so stability is an appearance rather than a fact.
heraclitus.note: Known only through fragments quoted by later writers.

classical-athens.summary: The democratic city-state of Socrates, Plato, Aeschylus and the Parthenon, whose institutions and ideas shaped later European thought.
